newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Experts doubt claim NZ state pensions can't work.
newsitem.headline: Experts doubt claim NZ state pensions can't work.

text.p: New Zealand experts on Tuesday cautioned against an overly simplistic approach to deciding whether the country's tax-payer funded pension system was sustainable.
The warnings come against a background of heated debate over merits of voluntary versus compulsory retirement savings, ahead of a September referendum on a mandatory superannuation scheme.
Prime Minister Jim Bolger has been accused of trying to scare people into voting for the scheme, after foreshadowing higher taxes or a cut in the State pension if voters reject compulsory savings.
He said the present system would become unsustainable as the 'baby boom' generation reached pension age next century.

Bolger claimed that by 2040 the number of workers per retired person would fall to two from the current five, and that the cost to the taxpayer of providing pensions would double in the next 40 years to 10 percent of GDP.
"The inevitability is we are going to have about a doubling of the number of retired New Zealanders in the future and it is clearly going to cost more for retirement income," Bolger said.
"We either prepare for that in savings or look to the increase of taxes or the reducing of benefits in the future."

However, NZ Institute of Economic Research (NZIER) director John Yeabsley told Reuters that while demographic changes were a concern that needed to be acknowledged, he would not place weight on simple worker-to-pensioner ratios.
"Just throwing around the ratio figures doesn't deal with the question. The ratios are suggestive but nothing like comprehensive," Yeabsley said.

Michael Littlewood, a member of the 1992 Todd Taskforce on retirement, says Bolger is simply trying to justify the referendum to satisfy December's coalition deal between his National Party and the NZ First Party, in which National agreed to hold a referendum on the issue.
The Todd Taskforce examined all the savings options and chose the present voluntary system as the most workable.
Littlewood told National Radio in April that Bolger's claims did not conform with the taskforce's 1992 research on retirement, which was updated by the NZIER in 1995.
"That (research) said that the scheme that we had, including the surcharge which has since been abolished, was broadly sustainable, albeit with some fiscal risks," Littlewood said.
NZIER's Diana Cook, who wrote the 1995 analysis, told National Radio the current scheme is sustainable.
"(It is) true that our population is ageing and this will have implications for the government expenses starting from around 2011.

"...But we actually did some analysis of this in 1995 and in our view we should be able to continue to pay national superannuation in line with the accord, without increasing taxes in the future," Cook said.
She added that was dependent on the government repaying debt now while it could, and maintaining reasonable levels of economic growth.
Since 1993 the National Party has been signatory to a multi-party accord which agreed to a formula for continued tax-funded pensions.
A spokesperson for Bolger said the Prime Minister's office was confident of the validity of the numbers used to back its claim that the current scheme was unsustainable.

Government statistician Len Cook told Reuters it could be deceptive to assume people over 65 were outside the workforce, as the Employment Contracts Act was likely to see more part-time labour by older people.
"We've actually created in New Zealand an environment where some of the very simple boundaries of what's old and young are really blurred quite massively," Cook said.
